title: First Battle of the Marne
summary: Seven days on the Ourcq, the two Morins and the marshes of Saint-Gond. Maunoury's 6th Army finds Kluck's open flank north-east of Meaux on 5 September; Kluck swings four corps back across the Marne to meet it and wins on the Ourcq, but every corps he moves widens the gap between his army and Bülow's, into which the BEF and Franchet d'Espèrey's 5th Army advance. Foch holds the marshes against Bülow's left and Hausen's night attack. On the evening of 8 September Moltke's emissary Hentsch reaches Bülow; on the morning of the 9th, with the British across the Marne, Bülow retreats and Hentsch tells Kluck to conform. The right wing marches for the Aisne.
outcome: German 1st and 2nd Armies retreat to the Aisne from 9 September; the Schlieffen timetable is dead and the mobile war in the West ends within the month.

events.title: Gronau meets Maunoury: the Ourcq opens
events.summary: North-east of Meaux, around Monthyon and Saint-Soupplets, the IV Reserve Corps — Kluck's flank guard — runs into the 55th and 56th Reserve Divisions leading Maunoury's advance out of Paris. Gronau attacks, then falls back in the night; Kluck learns that his open flank has been found.

events.title: Kluck recalls the II Corps across the Marne
events.summary: From his headquarters Kluck orders the II Corps back north over the Marne to the Ourcq — the first of four corps he will swing away from the BEF and the French 5th Army over the next three days.

events.title: Joffre's order of the day: the hour has come
events.summary: The general counter-offensive begins. Joffre's order of the day tells the armies that the battle on which the safety of the country depends has begun, that every effort must go to attacking and throwing back the enemy, and that troops which can no longer advance must hold the ground won at any price and be killed on the spot rather than fall back.

events.title: The BEF and the French 5th Army turn about
events.summary: After a fortnight's retreat the British and Franchet d'Espèrey's army face north again. The BEF advances from the Tournan–Rozay line towards the Grand Morin; the 5th Army attacks Kluck's III and IX Corps at Esternay — the corps Kluck is about to pull away to the Ourcq.

events.title: The taxis of the Marne leave Paris
events.summary: On Gallieni's order some 600 Paris taxis, requisitioned that afternoon, carry part of the 7th Division from Gagny and Livry to Nanteuil-le-Haudouin and Silly-le-Long in two runs through the night — four to five thousand men, a fraction of Maunoury's reinforcements, and the most famous image of the battle.

events.title: Hausen's night attack at Fère-Champenoise
events.summary: At three in the morning the Saxon XII Corps and the Guard go forward with the bayonet, without artillery preparation, against Foch's right at the eastern end of the marshes of Saint-Gond. The IX and XI Corps are driven back several kilometres and Fère-Champenoise is lost — the last German success of the battle.

events.title: Hentsch at Bülow's headquarters, Montmort
events.summary: Having visited the 5th, 4th and 3rd Army headquarters, Hentsch reaches Bülow at Montmort in the evening. Bülow and his staff judge the 2nd Army's position untenable once the BEF crosses the Marne into the gap; the two agree that if it does, the 2nd Army will retreat and the 1st must conform.

events.title: The BEF crosses the Marne
events.summary: The I and II Corps cross at Charly and Nanteuil-sur-Marne in the morning; at La Ferté-sous-Jouarre the bridges are down and the III Corps needs until the next day. German airmen report the British columns north of the river — the report that decides Bülow.

events.title: Bülow orders the 2nd Army to retreat
events.summary: With the British across the Marne on his open right, Bülow orders his army back behind the Marne towards Dormans and Épernay, and tells OHL and Kluck.

events.title: Hentsch at Kluck's headquarters, Mareuil: the 1st Army is to retreat
events.summary: Hentsch reaches Mareuil-sur-Ourcq late in the morning, after a drive through the retreating columns of the 2nd Army's right, and tells Kluck's chief of staff, Kuhl, that the 2nd Army is retreating and the 1st must fall back to the Aisne. Kluck, who believes he is winning on the Ourcq, obeys. Whether Hentsch had the authority — Vollmacht — to order it, and whether the battle was already lost, is the oldest dispute about the Marne.

events.title: The right wing stands on the Aisne
events.summary: After three days of pursuit the 1st and 2nd Armies are across the Aisne between Compiègne and Reims; when the Allies arrive on 13 September the Germans are dug in on the heights north of the river and the war of movement ends.

title: Liège
summary: Twelve Brialmont forts in a ring around the Meuse crossings, the first obstacle on the right wing's road. Emmich's six brigades try to rush the intervals on the night of 5/6 August and fail; Ludendorff, taking over a brigade whose commander has been killed, reaches the heights and bluffs the citadel into surrender on the 7th; Leman sends his field division away and fights on from the forts. They fall one by one from 8 August — Barchon first — and in a rush from the 12th, when the 42 cm and 30.5 cm howitzers arrive; Loncin explodes on the 15th with Leman inside; Hollogne and Flémalle give up on the 16th. Whether the defence cost the timetable anything is argued.
outcome: The city taken on 7 August, the forts by 16 August; the 1st and 2nd Armies march from the 18th. Leman a prisoner; the heavy howitzers' reputation made.

events.title: German troops cross the Belgian frontier at Gemmenich
events.summary: Belgium having refused passage on 3 August, Emmich's Army of the Meuse and Marwitz's cavalry cross the frontier near Gemmenich and Aachen on the morning of 4 August and close on the Meuse.

events.title: Emmich's demand refused; the bombardment begins
events.summary: A parlementaire's demand for free passage is refused by Leman; German field guns open on the eastern forts and Zeppelin L Z VI bombs the city on the night of 5/6 August.

events.title: The night assault on the intervals
events.summary: Five brigades attack the gaps between the forts in the dark and are thrown back with heavy loss — Rabosée, Retinne, the Ourthe; only the 14th Brigade, its commander Wussow killed and Ludendorff in his place, gets through to the heights above the city.

events.title: Leman sends the 3rd Division away
events.summary: With a German brigade on the heights and the intervals no longer tenable, Leman orders the 3rd Division back to the field army on the Gette and moves his own headquarters into Fort Loncin. The forts will fight on alone.

events.title: Ludendorff takes the citadel
events.summary: Ludendorff drives into the city with his brigade adjutant, hammers on the citadel gate and receives the surrender of its garrison; the city is German, the forts are not.

events.title: Fort de Barchon surrenders — the first
events.summary: Barchon, battered by 21 cm mortars and cut off, is the first of the twelve to give up.

events.title: The first 42 cm shell falls on Pontisse
events.summary: Krupp's M-Gerät, brought by road from Aachen, opens fire from Mortier; Pontisse is wrecked and surrenders the next day. The fortress, the strongest of its type in Europe, has met the weapon built to break it.

events.title: Pontisse, Embourg and Chaudfontaine fall
events.summary: Three forts in a day under the 42 cm and 30.5 cm howitzers; at Chaudfontaine the magazine explodes.

events.title: Fort de Loncin explodes; Leman taken
events.summary: A 42 cm shell reaches Loncin's magazine; the fort blows up with most of its garrison, and Leman is dug unconscious from the ruins and taken prisoner.

events.title: Visé burned
events.summary: The town of Visé on the Meuse, where the cavalry had crossed on 4 August, is sacked and burned by German troops on 15–16 August and some 600 of its people deported — one of the August massacres and burnings that Horne and Kramer trace to the franc-tireur panic.

events.title: Hollogne and Flémalle surrender — the last forts
events.summary: The last two forts on the left bank give up on the morning of 16 August; the road and railway through Liège are open, and the 1st and 2nd Armies begin their march on the 18th.

title: Lorraine — Morhange–Sarrebourg
summary: Plan XVII's main blow: the French 1st and 2nd Armies march into annexed Lorraine on 14 August towards Sarrebourg and Morhange, and the German 6th and 7th Armies give ground before them — the trap the 1905 memorandum had imagined, the French drawn east while the right wing wheeled behind them. Then Rupprecht, with OHL's leave, stops yielding: on 20 August the Bavarians strike the whole French front at Morhange–Sarrebourg and throw it back to the Meurthe in a day. The follow-up at the Trouée de Charmes on 24–25 August is held, and the left wing settles into a front before Nancy that will not move for four years.
outcome: The French offensive into Lorraine broken on 20 August; the German left wing's breakthrough at Charmes held on the 25th; the hinge at Metz secure — and two German armies that might have thickened the wheel committed to a battle the plan did not want.

events.title: Plan XVII opens: the 1st and 2nd Armies cross into Lorraine
events.summary: Dubail's 1st Army and Castelnau's 2nd advance into the annexed provinces — the offensive Plan XVII was built around — towards Sarrebourg and Morhange. Rupprecht's 6th Army and Heeringen's 7th fall back before them, as OHL's deployment intended.

events.title: OHL lets Rupprecht counter-attack
events.summary: Rupprecht and his chief of staff Krafft von Dellmensingen press to stop yielding and strike; Moltke's staff, after hesitation, lets them. The left wing is about to fight the battle Schlieffen's concept wanted it to avoid.

events.title: The 1st Army enters Sarrebourg
events.summary: The VIII Corps takes Sarrebourg as the Germans give ground; the advance is six days old and has met little more than rearguards.

events.title: Morhange–Sarrebourg: Rupprecht strikes
events.summary: At dawn the 6th Army's Bavarian corps and the 7th Army's XV and XXI Corps counter-attack the whole French front from Morhange to Sarrebourg, under artillery the French cannot answer. The XV Corps breaks; the XX Corps (Foch) holds on the Morhange heights while the army around it gives way; the 1st Army is thrown out of Sarrebourg.

events.title: Castelnau orders the 2nd Army back to the Meurthe
events.summary: By evening the 2nd Army is retreating on Nancy and the Meurthe; the 1st Army conforms on its right. Plan XVII's main offensive has lasted six days.

events.title: Lunéville falls to the Bavarians
events.summary: The 6th Army follows up across the Seille and the Meurthe; Lunéville is occupied on 22 August.

events.title: The Trouée de Charmes: Rupprecht tries the gap between Toul and Épinal
events.summary: Having won at Morhange, Rupprecht now asks to break through — the 6th and 7th Armies drive at the Charmes gap between the fortresses of Toul and Épinal, the door to the Moselle. Dubail and Castelnau, with Foch's XX Corps on the Grand Couronné, counter-attack into their flank on the 25th at Rozelieures.

sources.note: the 1st and 2nd Armies' orders and positions
the critique of the left wing's counter-attack

title: The Frontiers in the north — Charleroi, Mons, Le Cateau
summary: The German right wing meets the Allied left. Lanrezac's 5th Army, moved north into the angle of the Sambre and the Meuse, is forced off the Sambre at Charleroi by Bülow on 21–22 August and has Hausen across the Meuse at Dinant behind its right by the 23rd; the BEF fights its first battle on the Mons–Condé canal the same day; Lanrezac orders the retreat that night without telling the British. Namur falls on the 25th; Smith-Dorrien stands at Le Cateau on the 26th against orders and gets II Corps away; Joffre meets French and Lanrezac at Saint-Quentin. The Battle of the Frontiers is lost and the wheel seems to be working — and both Allied armies are still in being.
outcome: Both Allied armies beaten and intact; the retreat that became the Great Retreat; Kluck freed from Bülow and heading south-west, Lanrezac ordered to turn at Guise; Namur gone and Maubeuge invested.

formations.name: British 4th Division
formations.summary: Snow's division, landed in France on 23 August, reached the front in time to stand on II Corps' left at Le Cateau; it became the core of III Corps on 31 August.

formations.name: 19th Infantry Brigade
formations.summary: Formed from the lines-of-communication battalions at Valenciennes on 22 August; on the BEF's left at Mons and Le Cateau.

formations.name: Fortified position of Maubeuge
formations.summary: The French fortress on the Sambre, invested by the VII Reserve Corps from 25 August and held until 7 September — a corps the right wing would not have at the Marne.

events.title: The Sambre forced at Tamines and Auvelais
events.summary: Bülow's X Corps and Guard cross the Sambre east of Charleroi against Lanrezac's X Corps, which counter-attacks and is thrown back with heavy loss; the 5th Army is fighting in the angle of the Sambre and Meuse before the BEF is on its left.

events.title: The siege guns open on Namur
events.summary: The howitzers that broke Liège are at Namur within a week; the nine forts and the Belgian 4th Division will last four days.

events.title: Casteau: the BEF's first shots
events.summary: C Squadron, 4th Dragoon Guards, meets German cavalry on the Mons–Brussels road — the British army's first action on the Continent since Waterloo.

events.title: Charleroi: the 5th Army beaten on the Sambre
events.summary: Bülow's corps push the III and X Corps back from the river through the industrial suburbs; Lanrezac's counter-attack never starts. By evening the 5th Army's centre has given way.

events.title: Mons: Kluck attacks the BEF on the canal
events.summary: The 1st Army's III, IV and IX Corps come at Smith-Dorrien's II Corps along the Mons–Condé canal in close order and are shot down by rifle fire the Germans take for machine guns; by afternoon weight of numbers and the salient at Nimy force II Corps back a few kilometres. Haig's I Corps on the right is hardly engaged.

events.title: Dinant: Hausen's Saxons cross the Meuse
events.summary: The XII Corps forces the Meuse at Dinant against Franchet d'Espèrey's I Corps, which counter-attacks at Onhaye; in the town the Saxons shoot 674 civilians — the worst of the August massacres in Belgium.

events.title: Lanrezac orders the retreat — without telling the British
events.summary: With Bülow across the Sambre and Hausen across the Meuse behind his right, Lanrezac orders the 5th Army back in the night; Sir John French learns of it from a liaison officer the next morning and never forgives him. The BEF must retreat too or be enveloped.

events.title: Namur's last forts fall
events.summary: The second Belgian fortress goes in four days; the Guard Reserve Corps that took it entrains the next morning for East Prussia.

events.title: Landrecies: I Corps fights in the dark
events.summary: Haig's headquarters and the 4th (Guards) Brigade are attacked in Landrecies by the IX Corps' advance guard; the confused night action persuades I Corps to keep retreating east of the Forest of Mormal, away from II Corps.

events.title: Smith-Dorrien decides to stand at Le Cateau
events.summary: At two in the morning, with his men exhausted, the 4th Division and 19th Brigade on his left and Allenby's cavalry unable to cover a retreat, Smith-Dorrien tells GHQ he will fight at daybreak — against Sir John French's order to continue the retirement.

events.title: Le Cateau
events.summary: II Corps, the 4th Division and the 19th Brigade fight the 1st Army's IV and III Corps and Marwitz's cavalry in the open from dawn to mid-afternoon, losing some 7,800 men and 38 guns, then break off and march away south; Kluck, believing he has beaten the whole BEF, turns south-west after a phantom.

events.title: Joffre meets Sir John French and Lanrezac at Saint-Quentin
events.summary: A bad-tempered conference: French complains of Lanrezac's silence, Lanrezac of the British; Joffre, who has just issued Instruction générale no 2, asks both to keep retreating in line and orders Lanrezac to turn and strike at Guise.

events.title: Kluck released from Bülow's command
events.summary: OHL ends the subordination of the 1st Army to the 2nd that had chafed since 17 August; Kluck is free to march south-west — and will be asked to wheel back in three days later.

title: Guise / Saint-Quentin
summary: Joffre, building a new army on the left by rail and needing a day, orders Lanrezac to turn the retreating 5th Army and strike west towards Saint-Quentin. On 29 August the blow meant for Kluck lands on Bülow: the French left is stopped on the Ribemont road, Bülow's Guard and X Corps cross the Oise at Guise, and in the afternoon Franchet d'Espèrey's I Corps counter-attacks and throws the Guard back over the river. Lanrezac disengages the next morning. Bülow, checked, asks Kluck to wheel inward to help him — and the 1st Army turns south-east, inside Paris.
outcome: A day gained for Joffre's redeployment and the 5th Army kept intact; Bülow checked; Kluck asked to wheel in — the operational cause of the turn inside Paris and of the Marne; Lanrezac relieved on 3 September nonetheless, Franchet d'Espèrey in his place.

events.title: Joffre at Marle: the 5th Army is to turn and strike towards Saint-Quentin
events.summary: Joffre drives to Lanrezac's headquarters and orders him to attack westward with his whole army against the German forces pressing the British — a blow to relieve the BEF and gain a day for the new army forming on the left. Lanrezac, who sees the 2nd Army on his right flank, objects and obeys.

events.title: Haig offers I Corps; GHQ refuses
events.summary: Haig proposes to support the French attack with his corps on the 29th; Sir John French, set on getting the BEF out of the line, countermands it. Lanrezac's left will attack alone.

events.title: The 5th Army attacks towards Saint-Quentin
events.summary: The XVIII and III Corps go forward along the Ribemont–Saint-Quentin road and are stopped by Bülow's X Reserve Corps; the blow meant for Kluck lands on Bülow.

events.title: The Guard and X Corps cross the Oise at Guise
events.summary: While the French left is held, Bülow's Guard and X Corps come over the Oise at Guise against the French X Corps and the army's right, which bends.

events.title: Franchet d'Espèrey counter-attacks at Guise
events.summary: Lanrezac throws in the I Corps, brought across from the right; Franchet d'Espèrey leads it forward in the afternoon with bands playing, drives the Guard back over the Oise and retakes the crossings — the moment that makes his reputation and, three days later, gives him the army.

events.title: Bülow claims a victory and halts for a day
events.summary: The 2nd Army reports the French beaten and asks for a day's rest to recover; it has been checked on the Oise and its right has been hit.

events.title: Lanrezac breaks off and resumes the retreat
events.summary: Having gained the day Joffre asked for, Lanrezac disengages on Joffre's order and the 5th Army falls back on Laon and the Aisne.

events.title: Bülow asks Kluck to wheel inward
events.summary: To exploit the 'victory' and help his checked army, Bülow asks the 1st Army to wheel in towards the Oise and the Marne — the request that turns Kluck south-east, inside Paris, and opens the flank Maunoury will strike on 5 September. The counter-attack at Guise is the operational cause of the turn.

title: Belgium beyond Liège
summary: What the right wing left behind it. The Belgian field army, ordered back from the Gette on 18 August, is inside the Antwerp forts by the 20th, and Beseler's III Reserve Corps turns off the wheel to watch it; the IX Reserve Corps joins it at the end of the month. Namur falls in four days (21–25 August), Maubeuge holds for thirteen (25 August – 7 September) and keeps the VII Reserve Corps out of the Marne. The field army comes out twice — on 25–26 August and 9–13 September — to pin what it can. Behind the front the reprisals at Aarschot, Tamines, Dinant and Louvain, and the demolitions that kept the railheads a hundred kilometres behind the marching corps.
outcome: Two corps held in front of Antwerp and one at Maubeuge through the decisive week; the VII Reserve Corps reaches the Aisne on 13 September, a day after the Marne; the railways through Belgium still in repair. Belgium — 'the rape of Belgium' in the neutral press — becomes the moral case against Germany for the rest of the war.

formations.name: Marine Division
formations.summary: Naval infantry sent up from the coast at the end of August to take over part of the line facing Antwerp, with Landwehr brigades, so that the IX Reserve Corps could march south. Under Beseler for the siege in October.

routes.derivation: Edmonds vol. II for the withdrawal from the Gette (ordered on the 18th, complete on the 20th) and the two sorties: 25–26 August towards Hofstade and Elewijt between Malines and Louvain; 9–13 September to Aarschot and the edge of Louvain. Centre of the field army at the times shown; divisional positions are not drawn.
routes.notes: The token stands for four to five divisions out of six: the 4th was at Namur and then on its way round by France, the 2nd and parts of the 5th were fortress garrison at times.

routes.derivation: Michel's division left the Namur intervals on the night of 23/24 August behind the French 5th Army, went by rail through France to Le Havre, by sea to Ostend (27 August) and back to the field army at Antwerp; dates for the French legs from Tyng and Edmonds. Drawn as a transfer — the dashed line is the journey, not the track, and its first leg was a march.
routes.notes: The 4th Division's march out and journey round is the whole Belgian chapter in miniature: it could not hold Namur and it could not be spared, so it went the long way to the redoubt.

routes.derivation: Corps centre, approximate: on the 1st Army's northern flank through Aarschot on the 19th, turned north of Brussels on 20 August to face Antwerp, on the Vilvoorde–Louvain line for both sorties. From the Reichsarchiv narrative as summarised by Herwig and Edmonds; positions to a town and a day.
routes.notes: The corps that the tally shows leaving the wheel on 20 August. It never rejoined it: Antwerp in October, then the Yser.

routes.derivation: Detrained at Brussels on 27–28 August after release from Schleswig; took over part of the Antwerp front; released south in the first days of September as the Marine Division and Landwehr came up, and reached the 1st Army's right on the Ourcq, near Nanteuil, on 9 September. Herwig and Edmonds; the march itself is schematic.
routes.notes: The one masking corps that did get to the Marne — on its last day.

routes.derivation: On the 2nd Army's right from the Meuse below Liège to the Sambre west of Charleroi, then to the investment of Maubeuge on 25 August (the ring closed on the 26th), in place until the surrender on 7 September, then by Laon to the Chemin des Dames, reached on the morning of 13 September after about sixty kilometres in twenty-four hours. Herwig, Edmonds and Tyng; positions to a town and a day.
routes.notes: Zwehl's forced march filled the gap between the 1st and 2nd Armies on the Aisne ridge hours before the BEF's I Corps reached it — the corps the right wing had lacked at the Marne arriving one battle late.

routes.derivation: Holding part of the line west and north of Brussels from the end of August; a representative position.
The fortress; the token marks the city, the forts lay in two rings around it.

events.title: The King orders the field army back to Antwerp
events.summary: With the German 1st Army over the Gette in strength and no French or British force within reach, Albert orders the field army to break off and withdraw into the national redoubt — keeping the army in being rather than losing it in front of Brussels.

events.title: Aarschot: the first large reprisal
events.summary: German troops entering the town after a fight with the Belgian rearguard shoot 156 inhabitants and burn much of it, the pattern — a belief in civilian snipers, then collective punishment — repeated across Belgium in the next ten days.

events.title: Brussels occupied; the III Reserve Corps turns off
events.summary: The 1st Army marches through the open city and keeps wheeling south-west; Beseler's III Reserve Corps turns north instead, to stand between the Belgian field army and the roads and railways behind the wheel.

events.title: The field army is inside Antwerp
events.summary: Four divisions and the cavalry are inside the outer forts by evening on the 20th; the 4th Division is still at Namur.

events.title: The siege of Namur
events.summary: Gallwitz's Guard Reserve and XI Corps with the heavy howitzers from Liège: the bombardment opens on the 21st, Cognelée and Marchovelette fall on the 23rd, Michel's 4th Division slips out that night, and the last forts surrender on the 25th — four days, against the weeks the French had counted on.

events.title: Tamines
events.summary: After the 2nd Army's crossing of the Sambre, 383 townspeople are shot on the riverbank; the largest of the Sambre reprisals.

events.title: Dinant
events.summary: Hausen's Saxons, forcing the Meuse under fire and believing the town in arms, kill 674 civilians — the largest single reprisal of the invasion — and burn the centre.

events.title: The first sortie: Malines towards Louvain
events.summary: Four divisions out of Malines towards Hofstade, Elewijt and the Louvain railway, to hold German strength in the north while the French and British fight on the Sambre; the III Reserve Corps holds, the Allied retreat is reported, and the army is back behind the forts on the 26th.

events.title: The VII Reserve Corps invests Maubeuge
events.summary: Zwehl's corps, with a division of the VII Corps and the siege guns coming on from Namur, closes round the fortress; the BEF has just passed it, refusing to be shut in. The bombardment proper begins on the 29th.

events.title: Louvain burns
events.summary: At dusk on the 25th troops falling back from the sortie meet others arriving; shots are fired in the dark and the garrison concludes the town has risen. Over three days 248 inhabitants are killed, the library and some 1,100 buildings burned, and the population driven out. Horne and Kramer: no evidence of a civilian rising — a panic, and a doctrine that expected francs-tireurs.

events.title: The IX Reserve Corps detrains at Brussels
events.summary: Released from Schleswig once a British landing on the North Sea coast was ruled out; it takes over part of the front facing Antwerp.

events.title: The siege guns open on Maubeuge
events.summary: The 30.5 cm and 42 cm batteries that broke Liège and Namur begin on the Maubeuge forts; they hold nine days more.

events.title: The IX Reserve Corps marches for the Marne
events.summary: Relieved in front of Antwerp by the Marine Division and Landwehr, the corps is called south to the 1st Army; it reaches the Ourcq on the 9th.

events.title: Maubeuge surrenders
events.summary: Fournier surrenders the fortress and its garrison — some forty thousand men and four hundred guns by the British count; Herwig gives 32,700 prisoners, Lodier 45,000 — after thirteen days. The VII Reserve Corps is released.

events.title: The second sortie: Aarschot and the edge of Louvain
events.summary: Timed to help the Allied counter-offensive on the Marne: the Demer and Dyle crossings are taken, Aarschot retaken, the cavalry reaches the outskirts of Louvain on the 10th; the Germans turn the 6th Reserve Division back north and bring a division of the XV Corps from Alsace, and the field army is back inside the forts on the 13th.

events.title: The VII Reserve Corps reaches the Chemin des Dames
events.summary: After the surrender Zwehl marches by Laon and covers about sixty kilometres in the last day and night, arriving on the Aisne ridge on the morning of the 13th — in the gap between Kluck and Bülow, hours before the BEF's I Corps climbs towards it. The corps the wheel had lacked on the Ourcq arrives one battle late, and the Aisne holds.

title: The Ardennes: the encounter battles
summary: Joffre's main offensive under Plan XVII: the French 3rd and 4th Armies marched north-east into the wooded Ardennes on 21 August believing the German centre was thin, and on the 22nd met the German 4th and 5th Armies marching south-west through the same forest. A chapter, not a zoom-in — the campaign tokens keep moving on their campaign routes and these are static markers on the ground where the encounter battles were fought.
outcome: Both French armies were fought to a standstill in a single day and fell back to the Meuse on 23–24 August, opening the flank of Lanrezac's 5th Army at Charleroi and ending Plan XVII as an offensive. The heaviest single loss was the Colonial Corps at Rossignol — 11,648 men, its divisional commander and most of its officers — in an afternoon.[^greenhalgh-2014] Three-day totals for the two armies are unreliable (the returns were made in a retreat, and the missing were counted twice or not at all); the French army's own monthly return for August, which covers the Ardennes along with Lorraine and the Sambre, is carried as a single record in the human-cost ledger.[^herwig-2009] Ruffey was relieved of the 3rd Army on 30 August.

events.title: The French armies enter the forest
events.summary: Under Joffre's Instruction particulière no 13 the 3rd and 4th Armies advance north-east on a front of some eighty kilometres, with orders to attack whatever they meet. Cavalry reconnaissance in the wooded country tells them almost nothing, and aircraft are grounded by the weather.[^afgg-1-1]

events.title: Rossignol: the 3rd Colonial Division destroyed
events.summary: The 3rd Colonial Division of the 4th Army's Colonial Corps marches into the German VI Corps north of Tintigny. Its commander, General Raffenel, is killed with his brigade commander Rondony; the Colonial Corps loses 11,648 men in the day.[^greenhalgh-2014]

events.title: Bertrix: the 4th Army's centre broken
events.summary: XVII Corps is caught in column in the woods south of Bertrix by the German 21st Division and driven back with the loss of much of its divisional artillery — guns that could not be brought into action on forest tracks.[^zuber-2007]

events.title: Maissin and Anloy
events.summary: On the 4th Army's left, XI and XII Corps take Maissin and Anloy at heavy cost and hold them into the evening — the one part of the line where the French end the day on the ground they attacked for, and they abandon it the next morning with the rest.[^afgg-1-1]

events.title: Ethe and Bleid
events.summary: In fog on the 3rd Army's front, French and German columns collide at fifty metres in the village streets of Ethe and Bleid. The fighting lasts all day and is followed by German reprisals against the villagers.[^zuber-2007] [^horne-kramer-2001]

events.title: Virton
events.summary: V Corps is stopped in front of Virton by German artillery firing from the heights it had expected to occupy; the 3rd Army's attack towards Neufchâteau never develops.[^afgg-1-1]

events.title: Back to the Meuse
events.summary: Joffre orders the offensive resumed on the 23rd; neither army can. By nightfall both are falling back on the Meuse and the Semois, and on the 24th the retreat is general — uncovering the right of Lanrezac's 5th Army, already fighting at Charleroi.[^afgg-1-1] [^herwig-2009]

title: The Grand Couronné de Nancy: the hinge holds
summary: The heights east and north of Nancy, held by Castelnau's 2nd Army from the retreat out of Lorraine until the Germans gave them up after the Marne. A chapter, not a zoom-in: static markers on the ground the fighting was for, with the campaign tokens still moving on their campaign routes.
outcome: The position held through Rupprecht's offensive of 4–10 September while Castelnau sent two of his corps west by rail, and the German 6th and 7th Armies — the strongest concentration of German force in the west after the right wing — spent September attacking fortified heights instead of reinforcing the wheel. The Germans withdrew behind the Seille on 11–12 September; the line there barely moved again until 1918.

events.title: The 2nd Army digs in on the heights
events.summary: Thrown out of Lorraine at Morhange, Castelnau's army falls back onto the Grand Couronné — the ridge of wooded hills covering Nancy from the east — and entrenches. Joffre had wanted Nancy covered, not held to the last; Castelnau holds it.[^afgg-1-1]

events.title: Two corps leave for the west by rail
events.summary: XVIII Corps has already gone to the 5th Army on the Sambre; IX Corps entrains for the 4th Army. Castelnau is to hold the hinge with what is left — the argument the whole pack turns on, seen from the other end.[^afgg-1-1] [^doughty-2005]

events.title: Rupprecht's offensive opens
events.summary: The German 6th Army attacks the whole position, with the main weight against the forest of Champenoux and the Amance plateau, on the day Kluck's turn south-east is being read at Paris.[^afgg-1-1] [^herwig-2009]

events.title: The bombardment of the Amance plateau
events.summary: More than three thousand heavy shells fall on the Amance plateau in eight hours; the infantry attacks that follow do not carry it. It is the heaviest concentration of German artillery in Lorraine, fired on the day the Marne begins two hundred kilometres to the west.[^afgg-1-1]

events.title: Sainte-Geneviève
events.summary: The last coordinated German assault, on the northern hinge of the position above the Moselle. It is badly put together, goes in piecemeal, and fails.[^afgg-1-1]

events.title: Nancy shelled from Réméréville
events.summary: Sixty-seven heavy shells fall on the centre of Nancy, killing eight civilians. The bombardment is cover: the guns are firing to mask a withdrawal that has already begun.[^afgg-1-1] [^wikipedia-en]

sources.note: shell count and civilian dead, from the French account; verify against AFGG I/2 in the sourcing pass (sand-1l0.16)

events.title: The Germans go back behind the Seille
events.summary: The 6th Army pulls back east of the Seille, and French patrols find the forest empty. The front settles on that line and stays there, almost unchanged, until 1918.[^afgg-1-1] [^tyng-1935]

title: Origins of the plan: the two-front problem
summary: Why the German army of 1914 had one plan and it faced west. A chapter, not a zoom-in, and unlike the other chapters it narrates decades rather than days: Bismarck's alliances and their lapse, the Franco-Russian alliance that made the two-front problem real, Schlieffen's answer and the December 1905 memorandum, the French fortress line that closed the direct road, the younger Moltke's changes, Plan XVII and the cult of the offensive, Belgian neutrality, and the mobilization timetables that turned all of it into a machine. It carries no formations, routes or events of its own; what the map shows is the ground the argument is about - the fortress line from Verdun to Belfort, the Meuse at Liege and Namur, and the open country north of the Ardennes that the plan was built to use.
outcome: Two things go into the campaign from here. The first is a schedule: beat France in about six weeks by a right-wing sweep through Belgium, then turn east - the timetable the pack's two clocks measure everything against. The second is an argument that has never been settled: whether 'the Schlieffen Plan' was an operational plan the German army carried out in 1914, or a staff study for forces Germany never had, turned into a plan afterwards by men explaining a defeat. This chapter states both cases and leaves the question where the historians leave it.

title: The eastern cross-reference: two corps that fought in neither battle
summary: The other end of the same war. While the right wing swung through Belgium, one German army held East Prussia against two Russian ones; when it was checked at Gumbinnen on 20 August its commander proposed abandoning the province, and the alarm reached Moltke as the West seemed already won. On 25 August he took the Guard Reserve and XI Corps off the wheel and sent them east. A chapter, not a zoom-in: these are static markers on the ground where the eastern battles were fought, and the campaign tokens in the West keep moving on their own routes.
outcome: The Eighth Army, under Hindenburg and Ludendorff from 23 August and working to a concentration Hoffmann had already begun, encircled Samsonov's Second Army at Tannenberg on 26-30 August and took some 92,000 prisoners; Samsonov shot himself in the forest near Willenberg in the early hours of the 30th. Russian losses in killed and wounded are given anywhere between 50,000 and 78,000, and the totals are unreliable because only part of the army was inside the ring.[^showalter-2004] [^stone-1975] The two corps from the West were formally assigned to Hindenburg on 31 August - the day after the battle ended. They fought at the Masurian Lakes on 7-14 September, in the same week the Marne was lost without them.[^showalter-2004] [^herwig-2009]

events.title: Gumbinnen: the Eighth Army checked
events.summary: Attacking Rennenkampf's First Army in the open, the German Eighth Army is fought to a standstill and I Corps falls back in disorder. Tactically the day is indecisive; its consequence is entirely a matter of nerve.[^showalter-2004]

events.title: Prittwitz proposes to give up East Prussia
events.summary: That evening Prittwitz telephones OHL to say he intends to break off and retire behind the Vistula - abandoning the province, Königsberg and the ground the whole eastern deployment was built to hold. He is talked partly round within hours, but the alarm has been raised and cannot be unraised.[^showalter-2004] [^mombauer-2001]

events.title: Hindenburg and Ludendorff take over at Marienburg
events.summary: Moltke relieves Prittwitz on 22 August, sends for Hindenburg out of retirement and gives him Ludendorff - fresh from Liège - as chief of staff. They reach Marienburg on the afternoon of the 23rd and adopt the concentration against Samsonov that Hoffmann and the army staff have already set in motion.[^showalter-2004] [^stone-1975]

events.title: Tannenberg: the Second Army encircled
events.summary: The Eighth Army leaves a screen in front of Rennenkampf, moves the rest of itself by rail and road across the front of one Russian army to fall on the other, and closes a ring round Samsonov's centre. Some 92,000 prisoners are taken. Hindenburg asks that the battle be named for Tannenberg, where the Teutonic Knights were beaten in 1410; Ludendorff and Hoffmann each later claimed the idea.[^showalter-2004] [^stone-1975]

events.title: Samsonov walks into the forest
events.summary: Separated from his staff near Willenberg and unwilling to report the loss of his army to the Tsar, Samsonov shoots himself in the early hours of 30 August. A German patrol finds the body later.[^showalter-2004]

sources.note: date and circumstances; Old Style 17 August

events.title: The corps from the West are assigned - on 31 August
events.summary: Hindenburg is given the XI Corps, the Guard Reserve Corps and the 8th Cavalry Division for operations in East Prussia. The battle they were sent for ended the day before.[^showalter-2004]

events.title: The Masurian Lakes: the battle they did fight
events.summary: With the corps from the West now in the line, the Eighth Army turns on Rennenkampf and pushes the First Army out of East Prussia. It is fought in the same week as the Marne, thirteen hundred kilometres away, where the wing those corps came from is short of exactly what it lent.[^showalter-2004] [^stone-1975]
